top.line: Generative AI could amplify the food supply chain
top.para: Prompted by BBC Radio 4's The Cost of Food and its call for new ideas, I argue that generative AI used well amplifies the supply chain, where the cost of living is decided. A chain of encrypted vaults, one per party, could lower prices, and openness is the other half of the case.

s0.line: Joined records, not platforms, could break the buyer's chokepoint
s0.para: Food chains run on spreadsheets and the FAO counts 13% of food lost before retail, while big buyers holding a farm's output name the price, leaving 3p on £2.20 apples. One encrypted vault per party, joined by append lanes and a graph, plus models used only to build tools, could cut prices.

s1.line: Farmers keep almost nothing; records are retyped five times
s1.para: Sustain's 2022 study found a grower made 3p profit on a £2.20 kilo of apples and a wheat farmer 0.09p on a £1.14 loaf. Two thirds of companies treat Excel as a supply chain system, and the FAO puts food lost before retail at 13.3% in 2023, much of it from missing information.

s2.line: Big buyers name prices, and regulation leaves growers unarmed
s2.para: Once a buyer holds 20 to 40% of a farm's output it can set the price, the chokepoint Giblin and Doctorow describe, from ordinary practice, not malice. The Groceries Code Adjudicator and fair dealing rules for milk and pigs help, but they regulate the buyer and give the grower no forecast, second buyer or tool.

s3.line: The chokepoint is information; logistics is a data problem
s3.para: What gives the buyer power is knowing demand, rival prices, accepted grades and payment dates. Every step from field to shelf is records moving between parties, which generative AI is good at capturing, structuring and documenting. Fractal Semantic Graphs address exactly this: many parties, separate vocabularies, and a need to connect anyway.

s4.line: One encrypted vault per party, joined by lanes
s4.para: Each party holds its own vault; orders, delivery notes, grades and payments travel as files through write-only append lanes, and typed graph edges join vocabularies so waste becomes visible. Records are typed once, with no platform in the middle. It will not stop a dominant buyer naming a price, but it makes alternatives visible and cheap.

s5.line: Use the model to build tools, not run them
s5.para: A grower describes their piece of the chain, an agent builds a tool in an afternoon, and a small villager company hardens and runs it for many growers. No model sits in production. The tool fits because it comes from the grower's words, costs almost nothing to run, and is open by default.

s6.line: Evidence supports large-firm gains; nobody has tested farms
s6.para: McKinsey reported in 2021 that early adopters of AI supply chain tools cut logistics costs 15% and inventory 35% and raised service levels 65%, but these are large firms. The FAO values food loss at about USD 400 billion a year. The farm-level effect is unmeasured, and government money should fund tooling rather than regulation.

s7.line: Falling goods prices from productivity are not harmful deflation
s7.para: Laptop, PC and tablet prices fell 76% between 2005 and 2016 without stopping purchases. The BIS found, over 140 years and 38 economies, a weak link between falling goods prices and lower growth; harmful deflations were in assets with debt. A cheaper loaf from less waste is a productivity gain, not a lost decade.

s8.line: The unseen cost is not sharing; open models compound
s8.para: People avoid sharing because it is hard and ideas seem precious, yet about 80% of industrial data is never used. Sharing whole journeys beats curated success stories. Open-weight models, which economies like China build on, run locally and safely, as the Two Loops paper and Qwen's 100,000 derivatives show, and enable models per industry and language.

s9.line: Every component exists on sgit; the chain does not
s9.para: Encrypted vaults, read keys, append lanes, cross-vault graphs and vault apps are all published, and this site is built the explorer-and-villager way. Nobody has yet run a grower, packer and buyer through a season on vaults, and the grading vocabularies and villager companies are missing. The article is the brief for that experiment.

s10.line: Sources: the studies, books and reports cited
s10.para: Sources include Sustain's Unpicking food prices, the FAO Food Loss Index, ONS price data, Giblin and Doctorow's Chokepoint Capitalism and Doctorow's Enshittification. Also cited are the Groceries Code Adjudicator survey, McKinsey, the BIS study of deflations, the European data strategy, the Two Loops paper, the DeepSeek-V3 report and ETH Zurich's Apertus.
